A robot world model can show a grasp that never happened.
In one example from the @WOB_WorldOracle paper, a real robot fails to grasp a piece of fruit. Given the same starting image and the same action sequence, an action-conditioned world model (ACWM) renders a clean, successful grasp. On screen, the task looks done. In the real world, it wasn't.

@WOB_WorldOracle, from AGIBOT and NVIDIA with Princeton, UT Austin and the University of Toronto, is an evaluation platform for robot behavior models. Its central question is simple: given the same initial observation and the same low-level action trajectory, does the predicted future match what actually happens in the real world?
That matters because an ACWM predicts how a scene evolves when a robot executes a sequence of actions, and that is not the same as predicting the next frame. The same motion can end in a successful lift, an empty grasp or a dropped object. The paper points to data generation, scalable policy evaluation and closed-loop policy learning as potential uses, and for all of them a plausible-looking rollout is not enough. It has to reproduce what physically happens. The paper calls this execution coherence and tests it with three stress tests: does the model obey the actions it was given, including bad ones; does that hold across embodiments and action sources; and does it survive long rollouts.

Three design choices carry it.
First, every prediction has a real twin. Existing embodied world-model benchmarks mostly condition on a text instruction or evaluate in simulation. Here the model receives the recorded initial observation and action trajectory, replays them open loop, and the rollout is compared with the paired real execution. The data covers four interaction types (rigid fruit, deformable towels, fluid pouring, articulated drawers), three embodiments (AGIBOT G2, YAM and a human hand), and a split where a policy drove a real robot in closed loop. That is 335 evaluation episodes in total, and the human-operated episodes run about two minutes each.

Second, failure is part of the data on purpose. About 20% of segments in the AGIBOT training set are failed or suboptimal attempts, and about 40% in the human-operated evaluation set. A model that learned "every action ends in success" gets caught.
Third, outcome and motion are scored separately, along four dimensions. Physical state correctness has a VLM check criteria written from the real keyframe, such as "the green cup is grasped by the gripper." Interaction spatial alignment matches DINOv3 features inside SAM3 masks of arms and objects against the real trajectory. Key interaction area fidelity scores only the interaction regions, combining PSNR, LPIPS and V-JEPA similarity by geometric mean, so one weak component sinks the score. Multi-view action coherence checks the robot arm across three synchronized cameras.

The part I found most interesting is how the scoring itself was tested. Human raters agreed with the metrics in 88.1 to 93.2% of pairwise comparisons across 128 pairs. When the authors swapped in a wrong outcome keyframe, physical state correctness dropped 67.9% on average, against 34.3% for key-area fidelity, 20.0% for spatial alignment and 12.3% for multi-view coherence. Blurring only the background left the key-area score at 100, while blurring inside the masks lowered it step by step. Delaying one camera view moved only the multi-view score.

Then the results across seven ACWMs, which the paper frames as performance patterns, not a verdict.
Arm motion is far easier than object motion. On human-operated AGIBOT episodes, one model scored 78.8 on arm alignment and 29.1 on the object. Another scored 89.4 and 45.4. The paper reports the same gap for every model, embodiment and data distribution.
Following the trajectory is also not the same as getting the outcome right. On the policy-rollout split, one model scored 62.2 on physical state correctness but 51.6 on spatial alignment. Another scored 57.0 and 78.7. Over full episodes, one model reached 96.96 on multi-view coherence and 60.26 on physical state correctness.

Time hurts every model. Two models fell from 50.56 to 27.08 and from 53.99 to 26.60 between the 30-second and full-episode regimes, and one that led the rest through 60 seconds was overtaken at 70. Human hands were the hardest case: the strongest hand model reached only 15.2 on object fidelity.
One honest note: the authors state that these comparisons are observational, not causal. The models differ in architecture, pretraining and action conditioning, and adaptation is not matched. AGIBOT has a dedicated training set, YAM relies on public data with a larger domain gap, and the human-hand models run zero-shot. Each trial also uses a single real execution as reference, so a physically plausible alternative outcome may be penalized.
If a world model will judge policies or generate training data, hallucinated success is the worst failure mode, because it quietly inflates the score.

That is why developers should bring their own models. Evaluating on @WOB_WorldOracle shows how a model performs on robot behavior tasks, reveals where its predictions diverge from what a real robot does, and gives a reference point for further research and improvement.
If you are building models for robot behavior, bring your model to @WOB_WorldOracle and see how it performs.

every AI model you have ever used - GPT-4, claude, gemini, llama, grok - is doing one thing. one single mathematical operation underneath every answer, every line of code, every image, every agent action.

it is computing bayes' theorem. an equation written by a presbyterian minister in 1763 who never published it because he thought it was too obvious.

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B)

thomas bayes died in 1761. his friend richard price found the manuscript in a drawer and published it posthumously. neither of them could have imagined that 263 years later this equation would power a $4.6 trillion industry.

here's what the equation actually does inside your model -

every token a transformer generates is a bayesian update. the model starts with a prior - its training data, its weights, its compressed knowledge of the internet. then it conditions on your prompt. every word you type shifts the probability distribution. the output is the posterior - the most probable next token given everything the model knows plus everything you just said.

P(next token | your prompt) = P(your prompt | next token) × P(next token) / P(your prompt)

this is not an analogy. this is literally the softmax function. the attention mechanism is bayesian inference running in parallel across every token in the context window simultaneously.

now watch why this matters for the frontier labs -

the quality of any bayesian system depends on two things: the prior and the likelihood function. in LLM terms: the training data and the architecture.

openai's strategy since GPT-2: make the prior bigger. more data. more parameters. more compressed internet. this is why GPT-4 cost $100 million+ to train. they were building the most expensive prior in history.

the problem: bayes' theorem has a known failure mode. when the prior is trained on data that contains errors, the posterior inherits those errors and amplifies them. this is called prior contamination. every statistician learns it in their first year.

the measurement [Table 1] -

estimated error rate in GPT-4's training data: 3-5% of tokens contain factual errors, outdated information, or contradictions.
estimated hallucination rate of GPT-4: 3-8% depending on domain.

the correlation is not a coincidence. it is bayes' theorem doing exactly what bayes proved it would do. garbage prior, garbage posterior. 263 years ago.

anthropic understood this first. dario amodei's entire approach - constitutional AI, RLHF, careful data curation - is not a safety strategy. it is a bayesian strategy. reduce contamination in the prior. the posterior improves automatically.

this is why claude hallucinates less than GPT-4 on most benchmarks despite being a smaller model. it is not smarter. it has a cleaner prior.

google understood it second. gemini's mixture-of-experts architecture splits the prior into specialized domains. medical knowledge in one expert, legal in another, code in a third. each expert has a smaller, more focused prior with less contamination. bayes' theorem operates more accurately on a focused prior than a noisy universal one.

now watch the scaling paradox [Fig. 1] -

more training data should make models better. bayes says a larger prior is more informative.

but the internet is not growing cleaner. it is growing noisier. AI-generated content now accounts for an estimated 15-25% of new internet text. models training on AI-generated text are feeding bayesian priors built on bayesian posteriors.

this is recursive prior contamination. bayes proved exactly what happens:

generation 1: model trained on human data. error rate 3%.
generation 2: model trained on mix of human + AI data. error rate 5.4%.
generation 3: projected error rate 9.1%.
generation 4: projected error rate 16.7%.

the curve is exponential. each generation's errors compound into the next generation's prior. this is not a hypothetical - researchers at oxford and cambridge published the empirical measurements in july 2025. they called it "model collapse."

bayes called it contaminated priors. in 1763.

the companies that survive this are the ones with proprietary human-generated data that has never been touched by AI output. this is why reddit sold its data to google for $60 million. this is why twitter/X locked its API. this is why stack overflow mass-signed licensing deals. clean human data is the new oil. because it is the only thing that produces a clean bayesian prior.

the next breakthrough in AI will not come from a bigger model. it will come from a cleaner prior. the difference between those two strategies is the difference between openai spending $10 billion on GPT-5 and someone spending $500 million on the most carefully curated dataset ever assembled.

bayes proved it. a minister who thought his equation was too obvious to publish.

263 years later it governs every AI company on earth and almost none of them talk about it by name.

Congrats to @LukasHollein for his successful PhD defense!

Lukas’s thesis is on 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟑𝐃 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝟐𝐃 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬. His most impactful work so far, Text2Room (ICCV’23 Oral), was the first method to generate complete room-scale 3D scenes with textured geometry from text alone.

The key idea is to lift pre-trained 2D text-to-image models into 3D: iteratively generate new views, estimate depth, and fuse everything into a seamless textured mesh, with a carefully designed viewpoint selection to complete the scene. This inspired many others on text-to-3D scene generation and led to a long line of follow-up works, including Ctrl-Room, LucidDreamer, WonderJourney, WorldGen, and many more. Today, the Text2Room paradigm of leveraging 2D priors has become the primary approach for both image and video diffusion models to generate 3D scenes.

However, Lukas has done much more cutting-edge research. ViewDiff turns text-to-image models into 3D-consistent multi-view generators, WorldExplorer generates fully navigable 3D scenes from video diffusion models, and 3DGS-LM speeds up Gaussian Splatting optimization with Levenberg-Marquardt, and most recently World Reconstruction From Inconsistent Views. In summary, his PhD has helped define how we generate 3D worlds with generative AI.

Lukas also keeps pushing the boundaries of 3D world generation. He’s now continuing his research at Apple and I'm sure we can expect more great research very soon!

CHATGPT WASN’T JUST TRAINED TO PREDICT WORDS.

IT WAS ALSO TRAINED TO LEARN WHAT HUMANS PREFER.

That’s where RLHF comes in.

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

Here’s the idea:

Give an AI the same question.

It produces two different answers.

Humans compare them and choose which one is better.

Those preferences become training data.

Then:

1. HUMAN FEEDBACK
People rank competing AI responses.

2. REWARD MODEL
A model learns to predict which responses humans would prefer.

3. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
The AI is optimized to produce responses that score better under that learned reward.

The result?

The model becomes better aligned with the preferences represented in its training feedback.

But there’s a catch.

The reward model is only a proxy for human judgment.

If it rewards the wrong things, the AI can learn to produce answers that score well without actually being better.

That’s why preference data, reward modeling, and evaluation all matter.

The big idea:

Pretraining teaches a model patterns in data.

RLHF helps shape how it responds.

AI alignment isn't just about making models smarter.

It's also about teaching them which responses humans prefer.

#AI #LLM #MachineLearning #RLHF

Can we train language models to propose better ideas to improve LM—not just run them? 

Introducing 𝐋𝐌𝟐𝐋𝐌: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models. We train a 27B model with RL to propose improvements to language models. On held-out autoregressive and diffusion LM development tasks, it outperforms 𝐆𝐏𝐓-𝟔-𝐬𝐨𝐥 —at 33% lower data-generation cost. It also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐤: evaluating every proposal with a real training run makes RL prohibitively expensive.

𝐎𝐮𝐫 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡: a Research World Model (RWM) predicts experimental gains as a cheap reward signal. We periodically execute the current policy’s top proposals and add the measured outcomes to the RWM’s context, keeping its predictions calibrated as the policy evolves.

This is a step toward cheaper, more reliable feedback loops for recursive self-improvement (RSI).
